failures.title: BMW S58TU2 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Excessive Oil Consumption - particularly under track/high‑load use
items.onset: Varies - reported from new on some units
items.whatHappens: The S58TU2 is a high‑performance twin‑turbo engine designed for sustained high‑RPM operation. Under track conditions, oil consumption can reach up to 0.7 litres per 1,000 miles due to increased turbocharger bearing demand and piston ring blow‑by. Some owners have reported oil pressure warnings and low oil levels between services. Sustained track sessions maintain oil temperatures above 110°C for extended periods, reducing viscosity and accelerating consumption.
items.repairVsReplace: This is typically a characteristic of the engine's high‑performance design rather than a defect. Regular oil level monitoring and top‑ups between services are the standard remedy. If consumption becomes severe (well above 0.7L/1,000 miles), a compression and leak‑down test (£120-£350) can identify whether piston rings or valve seals are the cause. Catastrophic oil starvation from a failed oil pump or damaged oil cooler can write off the engine completely - replacement is the only option. → Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Cooling System Stress - water pump and radiator vulnerabilities
items.whatHappens: The S58TU2 runs hot by design, equipped with three radiators and an additional cooler, plus a dedicated transmission oil cooling system. However, the high heat and pressure the cooling system endures can lead to water pump failures, radiator leaks, and thermostat issues. Coolant leaks are a known weak point on high‑performance BMW engines.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump and thermostat replacement typically resolves the issue (£500-£1,200 at an independent specialist). If overheating is ignored, head gasket failure or cylinder head damage can occur - at which point a full engine replacement becomes the more economical route. → Read our full cooling system failure guide

items.title: Turbocharger and Fuel System Issues
items.whatHappens: The S58's twin turbochargers are integral to its performance but can suffer from lack of lubrication or excessive heat, leading to turbo lag or failure. High‑pressure fuel pump (HPFP) and injector issues have also been reported, causing misfires and reduced performance.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbocharger replacement (£1,500-£3,500 per unit) or HPFP replacement (£800-£1,500) typically resolves these issues. If left unaddressed, fuel starvation or turbo failure can cause engine damage requiring full replacement.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S58TU2
variants.intro: The S58TU2 (often designated S58B30T0 or S58T in technical literature) is the Technical Update version of BMW's S58 engine, introduced from 2025 model year onward. It is commonly confused with: | Similar Code | What It Is | Link | |---|---|---| | S58B30T0 | First‑generation S58 (2019‑2024) - fitted to pre‑LCI G80 M3, G82 M4, F97 X3 M, F98 X4 M | BMW S58B30T0 engine | | S58B30O0 | Lower‑output S58 variant - fitted to base‑spec M3/M4 (non‑Competition) | BMW S58B30O0 engine | | B58B30M1 | Standard B58 TU engine - 333‑374 hp, fitted to non‑M 40i models | BMW B58B30M1 engine | How to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block, visible from the driver's side of the engine bay, and also appears on the V5C registration document and in the vehicle's VIN (digits 4‑7). If you're unsure, enter your registration above - we'll confirm your exact fitment. Why the difference matters: The S58TU2 features updated engine management, revised turbocharger calibration, and - in the 2025 M2 - an additional 20 bhp over the previous generation. Fitting a first‑generation S58 into a TU2‑spec vehicle is not a straight swap; the ECU calibration, cooling system plumbing, and emissions hardware differ significantly.

relatives.description: - the first‑generation S58 (2019‑2024) fitted to pre‑LCI G80 M3, G82 M4, F97 X3 M and F98 X4 M; it produces slightly less power in some variants and lacks the TU2’s refined ECU calibration and revised turbocharger hardware. If you have a pre‑2025 M car, this is the engine you need.

- the base‑spec S58 variant (non‑Competition) with lower output (473 bhp) found in some early M3/M4 and M2 CS models; it shares the same block but runs a milder tune and smaller turbochargers. If you're after a more cost‑effective used replacement, this may be an option - but always verify compatibility with your ECU and cooling system.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S58TU2 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S58TU2 can make sense for owners facing a failed unit on a car that's still under warranty or for those with a lower budget. However, used M‑division engines carry significant risk: you don't know the engine's track history, oil consumption patterns, or whether the cooling system has been stressed. Only consider a used unit with full service history, an oil analysis report, and a compression test from a BMW M specialist. Expect to pay £4,500-£7,500 for a used S58 unit.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: For most S58TU2 replacements, a professionally reconditioned unit is the right call. A proper recon addresses the engine's known weak points: the cooling system (water pump, thermostat, radiators) is overhauled, the turbochargers are inspected and rebuilt if necessary, the high‑pressure fuel pump is tested or replaced, and all gaskets and seals are renewed. With a 12‑24 month warranty, this is the lowest‑risk option for a £6,000-£10,000+ investment.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for this engine only when the original block is in good condition and the vehicle has significant sentimental or collector value - e.g. a low‑mileage M3 CS or a well‑specified M4. A performance‑oriented rebuild can include upgraded forged internals and larger turbos, but for most owners, a reconditioned exchange unit offers better value and less downtime. Expect £8,500-£14,000+ for a full rebuild.
